entries.definition: Checks the identity and health posture of a device, such as patch level or antivirus status, before letting it join the LAN, and quarantines or denies systems that fail policy.

Rewrites private internal IP addresses to one or more public addresses at a router or firewall, conserving IPv4 space and hiding internal addressing from outside hosts; on its own it is not a true security control.
A legal contract in which parties promise to keep shared confidential information secret, used with employees, vendors and partners to protect trade secrets and sensitive data.

Short-range wireless technology working within a few centimeters, used for contactless payments, badges and phone pairing; risks include eavesdropping, relay attacks and skimming by attackers who get physically close.

An application-aware filtering device that inspects traffic up to layer 7, combining stateful inspection with intrusion prevention, URL filtering and application identification so rules can target specific apps rather than just ports.

A passive sensor fed by a SPAN port or tap that watches traffic across a segment and raises alerts on signatures or anomalies without blocking anything; contrast with its inline prevention counterpart.
An inline device placed in the traffic path that inspects packets and can actively drop, reset or block malicious sessions in real time, unlike a passive sensor that only alerts.

U.S. federal agency that publishes widely used security guidance such as the Cybersecurity Framework, the SP 800-53 control catalog and the SP 800-61 incident handling guide, which many organizations adopt as baselines.
The default disk format on modern Windows volumes, supporting ACL-based permissions, auditing, journaling and EFS encryption; its alternate data streams can be abused to hide malicious content.
Legacy Microsoft challenge-response authentication protocol that relies on password hashes, leaving it open to pass-the-hash and relay attacks; Kerberos is preferred in Active Directory domains.

Synchronizes system clocks with authoritative sources over UDP port 123; accurate clocks are essential for correlating logs, validating certificates and Kerberos tickets, and reconstructing incident timelines.

Lets a client ask a certificate authority's responder whether one specific certificate is still good or has been revoked, a faster and lighter alternative to downloading a full CRL; stapling lets the server supply the answer.
A globally unique dotted-number string, such as 2.5.4.3, that names a specific attribute, algorithm or policy inside X.509 certificates and SNMP MIBs so software can interpret fields unambiguously.
Core software that manages hardware, memory and processes and provides services to applications; keeping it patched, hardened and minimally configured is a foundational security baseline.

Information gathered from publicly available sources such as websites, social media, DNS records and public filings, used by defenders for threat research and by attackers or penetration testers for reconnaissance.

Link-state interior routing protocol that calculates best routes with Dijkstra's algorithm within an autonomous system; neighbor authentication should be enabled so attackers cannot inject false route advertisements.

Hardware and software that monitors and controls physical processes such as manufacturing lines, power grids and pipelines; availability and safety usually outrank confidentiality, and many such systems cannot be patched easily.
Wireless delivery of firmware, software updates or configuration to phones, vehicles and IoT devices; updates must be signed and verified so attackers cannot push malicious images.

An XML-based standard for describing how to check a system's configuration state and test for specific flaws or missing patches, letting scanners from different vendors share the same machine-readable checks.
A password-protected binary container, usually with a .pfx extension, that bundles a certificate together with its private key and chain so they can be imported, exported or backed up as one file.

A decentralized model where each node acts as both client and server and shares data directly; such traffic can spread malware, leak data and bypass controls, and botnets use it for resilient command and control.

Cloud model where the provider manages the runtime, middleware and operating systems so customers only build and deploy their own applications and data; it sits between renting raw virtual machines and buying finished software.
A JavaScript file that tells browsers which proxy to use for each URL; attackers who tamper with it or spoof its discovery via WPAD can route victim web traffic through a malicious proxy.
A Linux and Unix framework that lets administrators stack interchangeable login checks, such as password, MFA or LDAP verification, through configuration files without rewriting each application.

Controls for administrator and other elevated accounts, such as password vaulting, just-in-time permissions, session recording and ephemeral credentials, that limit how and when powerful accounts can be used.
An outdated PPP login method that sends the username and password in cleartext, offering no protection against sniffing; it has been replaced by challenge-based or encrypted alternatives.
A form of NAT in which many internal hosts share a single public IP, with each session distinguished by a unique source port number; this is how most home and small-office routers reach the internet.
A key stretching function that applies a hash-based MAC to a secret and salt thousands of times, making brute-force and rainbow table attacks against stored credentials far slower.
An organization's own telephone switching system that routes calls internally and to outside lines; unsecured or misconfigured ones can be abused for toll fraud and eavesdropping.
A file format and process for recording raw network frames, as produced by tools like Wireshark and tcpdump, providing the most detailed evidence for analyzing attacks and troubleshooting traffic.

entries.expansion: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
entries.definition: Industry-mandated security requirements for any organization that stores, processes or transmits cardholder data, including network segmentation, encryption, access control and regular vulnerability scans.
A rack-mounted strip that feeds electricity to multiple servers and network devices, often with remote monitoring and per-outlet switching to support availability and allow remote power cycling.
The file format for Windows programs, DLLs and drivers; analysts inspect its headers, imports and sections during malware analysis to spot packing or suspicious capabilities.
An EAP method that first builds a TLS tunnel using only a server certificate, then protects an inner password-based exchange such as MSCHAPv2 inside it; common in enterprise Wi-Fi.
Any portable gadget an individual carries, such as a phone, tablet or smartwatch; such devices can bring data leakage, unauthorized recording or malware into secure areas unless governed by policy.
A Base64-encoded text format for certificates and keys, framed by BEGIN and END lines and widely used by web servers; the name survives from an early secure email proposal.
A key exchange property in which each session uses fresh ephemeral keys, so compromising a server's long-term private key later does not let attackers decrypt previously recorded sessions.
Encryption software for signing and encrypting email and files with public/private key pairs, relying on a decentralized web of trust between users rather than certificate authorities.

Medical records and health-related data linked to an identifiable patient, such as diagnoses, treatments and insurance details; in the U.S. it is regulated by HIPAA and requires strong confidentiality controls. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Personal Health Information".)

Any data that can single out a specific individual, alone or combined with other details, such as names, Social Security numbers or biometric records; its exposure triggers breach notification and privacy obligations.
A U.S. federal smart card standard (FIPS 201) holding certificates and biometric data, used by government employees and contractors for multifactor physical and logical access.
A family of numbered specifications originally published by RSA Laboratories that define formats for keys, certificate signing requests, signed messages and key containers, such as #7, #10 and #12.

The combined framework of certificate authorities, registration processes, certificates, revocation services and policies that binds public keys to identities and enables trust for TLS, signing and encryption.
A legacy mail retrieval protocol (version 3 on port 110) that downloads messages from a server to a client; it should be wrapped in TLS on port 995 to avoid exposing credentials in cleartext.
Traditional analog copper-line phone service still used for alarm panels, fax and out-of-band modem access, where unsecured dial-in lines can give attackers an overlooked entry point.
A data link layer protocol that establishes a direct connection between two nodes, such as over serial or dial-up links, and supports authentication methods like PAP and CHAP.
An old Microsoft VPN protocol that encapsulates PPP frames over GRE; its MS-CHAPv2 authentication and weak encryption are broken, so it should be replaced with IPsec or TLS-based VPNs.
A secret passphrase configured in advance on every device that must communicate, as in WPA2-Personal Wi-Fi; simple to deploy but hard to rotate and vulnerable if weak or widely shared.
Camera capability for remotely rotating horizontally, angling vertically and magnifying the image, letting security staff follow activity across a wide area from a single surveillance unit.

Bundled software such as adware, toolbars or browser hijackers that a user may technically consent to installing but that degrades privacy or performance; anti-malware tools often flag it at lower severity.
A designated account or person authorized to decrypt data or restore access when a user's encryption key is lost, as with EFS or key escrow arrangements, preventing permanent data loss.
A PKI component that verifies the identity of certificate requesters and approves requests on behalf of a certificate authority, which then actually issues and signs the certificate.

entries.expansion: Research and Development in Advanced Communications Technologies in Europe
entries.definition: A 1990s European Union telecommunications research program; its integrity evaluation project produced the RIPEMD hash family, which is why the name appears inside that hash's expansion.

An iterative software approach that favors quick prototyping and user feedback over lengthy upfront planning; security requirements must be built into each iteration so speed does not introduce vulnerabilities.
An AAA protocol over UDP that centralizes logins for VPN, 802.1X Wi-Fi and network devices; it encrypts only the password field, unlike TACACS+, which encrypts the whole payload.

Combining multiple drives so data is striped, mirrored or protected with parity for fault tolerance and availability; levels like 1, 5 and 6 survive drive failures, but none replaces backups. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Redundant Array of Inexpensive Disks".)
A server that accepts incoming connections from offsite users over dial-up or VPN links and authenticates them before granting entry to internal resources.

Malware that gives an attacker hidden administrative control of a victim's computer, often enabling keylogging, screen capture, file transfer and webcam spying while masquerading as legitimate software.
Permissions are assigned to job functions such as nurse or payroll clerk, and users gain rights by being placed in those groups, simplifying administration and supporting least privilege.
Access decisions are driven by system-enforced conditions set by an administrator, such as time-of-day limits or firewall ACL entries, applied uniformly regardless of the user's job function.
A fast stream cipher once used in WEP, WPA-TKIP and early TLS; serious keystream biases make it insecure, so it is deprecated in all modern protocols.

Microsoft's protocol for graphical remote control of Windows systems over TCP port 3389; exposed instances are prime targets for brute force and ransomware, so place it behind VPN, MFA and network-level authentication.

Tags read wirelessly for inventory, badges and toll payments; attackers can clone or skim many access badges from a short distance, so higher-security cards use encryption and mutual authentication. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Radio Frequency Identifier".)

entries.expansion: RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest
entries.definition: A European-developed cryptographic hash family whose 160-bit version is used in Bitcoin address generation and some PGP implementations; an alternative to the SHA family for integrity checking.
A financial measure comparing the benefit gained from a security purchase against its cost, used to justify spending on controls by showing that avoided losses exceed what the control costs.

The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, such as four hours, which dictates how often backups or replication must occur; unlike its sibling metric, it looks backward to the last good copy, not at downtime.
A widely used asymmetric algorithm whose security rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes, used for digital signatures, key exchange and certificate keys.
A DDoS mitigation technique in which routers or an ISP are signaled, usually via BGP, to drop all traffic destined for an attacked address, sacrificing that target to protect the rest of the network.

The maximum tolerable duration of an outage before a system must be restored to service; it drives recovery strategy choices, whereas its data-focused counterpart measures how much information can be lost.
A specialized kernel that guarantees tasks respond within strict deadlines, found in industrial controllers, vehicles and medical devices; many are hard to patch and lack modern security features.
Carries audio and video streams for VoIP and conferencing over UDP; it has no built-in encryption, so its secure variant should be used to prevent eavesdropping on calls.
Standard for digitally signing and encrypting email messages using X.509 certificates issued by a CA, providing sender authentication, integrity and confidentiality within mail clients.

Cloud model delivering complete, ready-to-use applications such as webmail or CRM over the internet, where the provider manages everything and the customer mainly handles user access and data settings.
The WPA3 password-based key exchange, built on the Dragonfly handshake, that replaces WPA2's PSK authentication, resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy for each session.

An XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication and authorization statements between an identity provider and a service provider, enabling federated web single sign-on across organizations. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Security Assertions Markup Language".)

A dedicated high-speed network giving servers block-level access to consolidated disk arrays, often over Fibre Channel or iSCSI; it should be isolated from user traffic and supports replication for resilience.
A certificate extension listing additional hostnames, IP addresses or email addresses the certificate is valid for, letting one certificate protect several domains.
A cloud-delivered architecture that converges SD-WAN networking with security functions like web gateways, CASB, ZTNA and firewalling, enforcing policy close to users wherever they connect.

Industrial control architecture in which central software gathers telemetry from remote sensors and PLCs across sites like utilities and pipelines and sends commands back; such systems are often legacy and should be segmented.
A NIST suite of standards, including OVAL, CVE, CVSS and XCCDF, that lets tools automatically check configuration compliance and vulnerabilities using shared machine-readable content.
A protocol that lets network devices and managed endpoints automatically request and receive certificates from a CA at scale, commonly used with MDM; it relies on a shared challenge password.

An overlay that centrally manages and steers branch traffic across multiple links such as broadband, LTE and MPLS based on application policy; security must be added through encryption and integrated firewalling.
A packaged set of libraries, APIs, documentation and tools for building applications on a platform; third-party ones embedded in apps can introduce vulnerabilities or excessive data collection.

The structured phases of building software, from requirements and design through coding, testing, deployment and maintenance; integrating security into every phase is cheaper than fixing flaws after release.
The particular process model an organization adopts for building software, such as waterfall, agile or spiral, which determines when security reviews, testing and approvals fit into the work.

An architecture that separates the control plane from the data plane so a central controller programs switches and routers through software, enabling dynamic segmentation but making the controller a high-value target.
A kernel security module, originally from the NSA, that enforces mandatory access control by labeling every process and file, confining compromised services even when they run as root.
Storage hardware with an onboard controller that transparently encrypts everything written to it using a built-in key, so contents are unreadable if the device is removed; Opal is a common standard.

Windows mechanism for handling program errors at runtime; overwriting its records on the stack is a classic buffer overflow exploitation technique, which compiler and operating system protections now mitigate.
Moves files over an SSH session on port 22, encrypting both credentials and contents in one channel; it is unrelated to FTP over TLS, which is a separate secure option.

A family of NIST-standardized one-way digest functions, with 256- and 512-bit variants widely used for integrity checking, digital signatures and certificates; the older 160-bit version is deprecated due to collisions. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Secure Hashing Algorithm".)
A largely abandoned 1990s approach that secured individual web messages at the application layer; it lost out to running ordinary web traffic inside TLS, which is what HTTPS does.
A platform that collects and normalizes logs from across the environment, correlates them in real time, raises alerts and retains records for investigation and compliance reporting.

A removable or embedded chip in a mobile device that stores the user's identity and keys for the cellular network; attackers who convince a carrier to move a number to their own chip can intercept SMS codes.
A contract with a provider that defines measurable performance commitments, such as uptime percentages and response times, along with penalties if the provider fails to meet them.
The monetary loss expected from one occurrence of a risk event, calculated as asset value times exposure factor; multiplying it by the annualized rate of occurrence yields ALE.
Cellular text messaging; it is a vector for smishing and, because texts can be intercepted or redirected through SIM swapping, it is a weak channel for one-time passcodes.

The protocol mail servers use to send and relay email, on port 25 between servers and 587 for client submission; it lacks encryption and sender verification by itself, relying on STARTTLS, SPF and DKIM.
Email submission or relay protected by implicit TLS, typically on port 465, so credentials and message content are encrypted from the start of the connection rather than upgraded later.
A protocol for monitoring and configuring network devices through polling and traps; versions 1 and 2c use cleartext community strings, so version 3 with authentication and encryption should be used.

An XML-based messaging protocol for web services that exchanges structured envelopes over HTTP, often secured with WS-Security; its parsers must be protected against XML injection and external entity attacks.
Platform that integrates security tools and uses playbooks to automatically triage alerts, enrich indicators and carry out containment actions, reducing analyst workload and response time.
A team and facility that monitors an organization's systems around the clock, triages alerts, hunts threats and coordinates incident response, typically using SIEM and related tooling.
A single integrated circuit that combines a processor, memory, graphics and radios, common in phones and IoT devices; firmware and hardware flaws in it can be difficult or impossible to patch.
A contract document detailing the specific tasks, deliverables, timelines and acceptance criteria for a project performed by a vendor, often tied to a master service agreement.
A DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send email for a domain, letting receiving servers detect spoofed senders; usually combined with DKIM and DMARC.
Unsolicited bulk messages delivered through instant messaging or chat platforms rather than email, often carrying phishing links or malware.
Standard language for querying and managing relational databases; applications that build these statements from unsanitized user input become vulnerable to injection.

An attack where crafted input alters a database statement built by an application, letting attackers read, modify or delete data or bypass logins; prevented with parameterized queries and input validation.
Adds encryption, message authentication and replay protection to voice and video streams, protecting VoIP calls and conferencing from eavesdropping and tampering.
Storage built on flash memory with no moving parts; wear-leveling means overwriting may not reach every cell, so secure sanitization relies on built-in secure erase or cryptographic erase.
Encrypted protocol on TCP port 22 for remote command-line administration, tunneling and file transfer, supporting key-based authentication; it replaces insecure Telnet and rlogin.
The original Netscape protocol for encrypting web sessions; all versions are now deprecated due to flaws like POODLE, and its successor TLS should be used even though the old name persists.
Authentication arrangement where one login grants access to multiple applications without re-entering credentials, improving usability but making that one account a high-value target that needs MFA.
A standardized JSON language for describing cyber threat intelligence, such as indicators, threat actors and campaigns, so organizations can share it consistently; it is often transported by TAXII.
A proxy-based service that filters users' outbound browsing, blocking malicious sites, enforcing acceptable use and data loss rules, and inspecting downloads, whether on-premises or cloud-delivered.

entries.expansion: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
entries.definition: Cisco-originated AAA protocol over TCP port 49 that separates authentication, authorization and accounting and encrypts the entire payload; often used to control administrator logins to network devices.

entries.expansion: Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information
entries.definition: A transport protocol over HTTPS that defines how threat intelligence is shared between servers and clients through collections and channels, usually carrying STIX-formatted content.

The foundational protocol suite of the internet, combining connection-oriented reliable delivery with packet addressing and routing; understanding its ports, handshakes and headers is essential for analyzing network attacks.
A Kerberos credential issued by the KDC after initial login that lets a user request service tickets without re-entering a password; stealing or forging one enables golden ticket attacks.
A WPA-era encryption method that wrapped RC4 with per-packet keying and integrity checks to patch WEP without new hardware; it is now deprecated in favor of AES-CCMP.

Cryptographic protocol securing data in transit for HTTPS, email and VPNs through certificate-based authentication and negotiated session keys; versions 1.2 and 1.3 are current, while older ones are deprecated.
The moment a program verifies a condition, such as a file's permissions; if the resource changes before it is actually used, a race condition lets attackers swap in something malicious.

Generates short-lived numeric codes from a shared secret and the current clock, typically changing every 30 seconds in authenticator apps; unlike HOTP, codes expire with the clock rather than advancing by counter.
The later moment a program actually acts on a resource it validated earlier; the gap between validation and this action is the window an attacker exploits in a race condition.
A secure cryptoprocessor on a motherboard that stores keys, measures boot integrity and supports features like BitLocker and attestation, protecting secrets from extraction by software.
A mechanism that authenticates DNS messages, such as zone transfers and dynamic updates, using a shared secret key and HMAC, preventing unauthorized servers from altering or pulling zone data.
Describes how an adversary operates, from high-level goals down to specific methods, as cataloged in MITRE ATT&CK; profiling these behaviors supports threat hunting and attribution.
Final testing phase in which end users or business owners confirm that a system meets their requirements in realistic scenarios before it is approved for production release.
A remotely piloted or autonomous aircraft, commonly called a drone; it can be used for surveillance or payload delivery near facilities, and its own control links and firmware can be attacked.

A connectionless transport protocol that sends packets without handshakes or delivery guarantees, used by DNS, VoIP and streaming; that lack of handshake makes source spoofing and amplification DDoS attacks easier.
Modern motherboard firmware replacing legacy BIOS that initializes hardware and launches the bootloader; its Secure Boot feature verifies signatures to block bootkits and rootkits.

A single console for managing and securing laptops, desktops, phones and IoT devices by enforcing configuration, patching and application policies; it extends mobile device management to every device type.

Battery-backed equipment that provides immediate short-term power during outages or sags, giving systems time to shut down gracefully or for generators to start. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Uninterruptable Power Supply".)
A string that identifies a resource by name or location, of which URLs and URNs are subtypes; attacker-crafted ones can carry injection payloads, traversal sequences or deceptive paths.

A web address specifying protocol, host and path; attackers use lookalike domains, shorteners and encoded characters in them for phishing, while web filters block categories of them. (CompTIA's acronym list writes it as "Universal Resource Locator".)

Standard interface for connecting peripherals and removable storage; malicious flash drives, keystroke-injection gadgets and juice-jacking chargers make these ports a threat vector best controlled by device policies.
A feature letting a phone or tablet act as a host for peripherals like flash drives and keyboards; it can bypass mobile data controls, so MDM policies may disable it.
An all-in-one security appliance that combines firewall, IPS, antivirus, content filtering, VPN and spam blocking in one box, convenient for small offices but a potential single point of failure.

Common copper network cabling such as Cat5e or Cat6 that lacks foil or braided protection, making it cheaper but more susceptible to electromagnetic interference and emanation eavesdropping than protected cable.
Scripting language embedded in Microsoft Office for automation macros; malicious documents commonly abuse it to download and run malware, which is why macros from the internet are blocked by default.

The hosted user workspace an employee actually sees, delivered from central servers and accessed remotely, so applications and data stay off the endpoint and the session can be reset to a clean image.

The back-end platform of hypervisors, connection brokers and storage that centrally hosts and streams many user desktops to thin clients or laptops, keeping data in the data center and simplifying patching.
Logical segmentation of a switched network into separate broadcast domains, isolating groups like voice, guests and servers; misconfigured trunk ports allow hopping attacks between segments.
Technique that lets subnets carved from one address block use different prefix lengths, sizing each segment to its needs and conserving addresses while supporting finer segmentation.
A software-emulated computer running its own OS on a hypervisor; risks include escape to the host, sprawl of unmanaged instances and resource reuse between tenants.

Carrying telephone calls as packets over data networks; it is exposed to eavesdropping, toll fraud, vishing and denial of service, so signaling and media should be encrypted and voice traffic segmented.
A logically isolated section of a public cloud where a customer defines its own subnets, routing, gateways and security groups to segment and protect workloads.
An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet that connects remote users or sites to internal resources, using protocols like IPsec, TLS or WireGuard.
Real-time audio and video meetings between remote participants; risks include uninvited attendees, recording leaks and unpatched clients, so meetings need passcodes, waiting rooms and encryption.
Filter in front of web servers that inspects HTTP requests and responses at layer 7 to block attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting using signatures and rules.

The device bridging Wi-Fi clients to the wired network; its placement, power levels and configuration, such as disabling WPS and using WPA3, determine coverage and resistance to rogue and evil twin attacks.
The original 802.11 encryption scheme, using RC4 with short initialization vectors; it can be cracked in minutes and must never be used.
Sensors that monitor the radio spectrum for rogue access points, evil twins, deauthentication floods and other Wi-Fi attacks and alert administrators without taking blocking action.
Extends Wi-Fi monitoring with active countermeasures, such as containing rogue access points or deauthenticating unauthorized clients, rather than merely alerting on suspicious radio activity.
An authorization document that directs specific maintenance or change tasks to be performed, tying technical work to an approved request so changes are tracked and accountable.
Family of wireless security protocols that replaced WEP; version 2 uses AES-CCMP and version 3 adds SAE, with Personal mode relying on a passphrase and Enterprise mode on 802.1X.
A push-button or PIN method for easily joining devices to a home wireless network; the eight-digit PIN can be brute-forced quickly, so the feature should be disabled.
A security layer adapted from TLS for 1990s-era mobile phone browsers, optimized for low bandwidth but with known weaknesses; it is now obsolete.

Security platform that correlates telemetry from endpoints, network, email, cloud and identity in one analytics engine to find threats and coordinate containment across layers, going beyond endpoint-only tools.
A text-based tagged format for structured data used by SAML, SOAP and configuration files; insecure parsers are exposed to injection and external entity (XXE) attacks.
A bitwise operation that outputs 1 only when its two inputs differ; it is a building block of stream ciphers and one-time pads and is sometimes used by malware for simple obfuscation.

A web attack that tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending an unwanted state-changing request to a trusted site, such as a funds transfer; anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies prevent it.

A web flaw where an application includes unsanitized user input in pages, letting attackers run malicious scripts in other users' browsers to steal sessions or deface content; output encoding and CSP mitigate it.
